items.text: WTI and Brent both spiked 10%+ overnight (WTI +9.6% to $91.48, Brent +8.8% to $96.02) on geopolitical tensions, mirroring the Iran conflict backdrop evident in late-August sentiment data. For credit investors: energy hedges embedded in HY and IG portfolios face mark-to-market pressure; refiners and importers see tighter margins, but energy names with pricing power (integrated oils, LNG) may offer relative value if crude stabilizes above $90.

July payrolls printed -23K (a surprise miss versus consensus +20K), marking the first negative print since early 2024 and signaling cooling labor demand. However, unemployment held at 4.1% and initial jobless claims remain low at 203K (vs 207K prior week), suggesting slack is gradual. For credit: watch for September ADP and ISM employment subindices on Sept 3–4 to confirm whether August was a soft patch or trend reversal; high-yield default risk rises if labor cracks faster.

1-year inflation expectations ticked up to 4.3% from 4.2% in July, driven by energy/commodity shocks and Middle East conflict spillovers. Core PCE (July) sits at 2.47% YoY, PPI at 4.66%, showing goods inflation still elevated despite headline CPI cooling to 3.3%. For credit: sticky core inflation may cap Fed cuts; real rates stay elevated, pressuring leveraged balance sheets and refinancing spreads if the curve inverts further.

ECB raised deposit rate 25 bps to 2.25% in June 2026, while the Fed funds rate stands at 3.75% with base case for no further 2026 hikes. UST 10Y jumped 13 bps to 4.79% and 2Y rose 20 bps to 4.39%, compressing the 2-10 curve to just 40 bps—now inverted in real terms. For credit: tighter monetary policy + inverted curve historically coincides with downgrades; IG/HY spreads face headwinds if growth expectations dim.

HY OAS widened 2 bps to 265 bps, IG OAS up 2 bps to 81 bps, while CCC OAS spiked 18 bps to 1049 bps—a significant stress signal in the distressed tier. The move correlates with equity weakness (VIX +89 bps to 16.34) and real rates. For credit investors: CCC dislocations present alpha opportunity but signal market is repricing tail risk; watch for cross-over spreads (BB-to-B) for refinancing walls in 2026–27.

China manufacturing PMI stayed in contraction at 49.8 in August (prior 49.2), better than consensus 49.6, while US ISM Mfg fell to 54.6 in August from 55.6 (consensus 55.2). GDPNow nowcast jumped to 4.8% from 1.54%, but this appears driven by Q2 base effects; Q2 actual GDP was only 1.5%. For credit: global growth deceleration risk remains—watch for Q3 US ISM PMI (due Sept 3) and China PMI (Sept 30) as leading indicators; recession odds are rising in forward expectations.

Michigan consumer sentiment fell sharply to 51.0 in early August from 55.2 in July, down from 55.2 in July and below forecast of 54.5, with sentiment ending two consecutive months of improvement and well below the 55.0 estimate. Existing home sales slipped to 4.06M SAAR (July), mortgage rates hold at 6.66%, and housing starts fell to 1.239M. For credit: consumer weakness + housing deceleration threatens non-prime auto, retail finance, and RMBS portfolios; refinancing pressure on consumer-facing corporates (retailers, restaurants) may emerge if sentiment stabilizes below 52.

themeCards.title: Middle East energy shock
themeCards.statusLine: WTI and Brent both spiked overnight on the Iran conflict, rising 9.6% and 8.8% respectively. Crude now trades near $91–$96, compressing downstream margins and inflating headline CPI expectations.
themeCards.relevance: Energy-exposed HY credits (E&P, shipping, chemicals, airlines) face immediate cash flow pressure. Hedging costs rising; refiners benefit short-term but face margin risk if conflict escalates. Watch for covenant stress in leveraged energy M&A.

themeCards.title: Inverted curve + sticky core inflation
themeCards.statusLine: 2-10 curve compressed to 40 bps; real rates positive (10Y real ~1.8%), yet core PCE remains sticky at 2.47% YoY. Fed unlikely to cut aggressively until inflation clearly breaks trend.
themeCards.relevance: Extended real rate shock pressures multiple arbitrage (CLO reinvestment, refinancing, M&A carry). High-yield credit duration extends as yields rise; IG spreads may not fully compensate if growth falters, creating cross-over opportunity in BB/B.

themeCards.title: Consumer sentiment cliff + inflation regime
themeCards.statusLine: University of Michigan sentiment fell to 51.0 from 55.2 in July, below forecast of 54.5, driven by energy/food cost shock and weakened business outlook. Year-ahead inflation expectations remain above 4%.
themeCards.relevance: Consumer-facing credits (retail, restaurant, discretionary finance) facing multiple headwinds: purchasing power erosion, sentiment collapse, and mortgage/auto rate lock-in. Credit quality deteriorates if employment rolls over; watch Q3 earnings guidance on consumer health.

themeCards.title: Global growth deceleration signal
themeCards.statusLine: China manufacturing PMI at 49.8 (below 50 for second month), US ISM Mfg 54.6 (consensus miss). Forward indices (orders, expectations) weakening sharply—especially in China where confidence fell to lowest since election.
themeCards.relevance: Cyclical credit (industrials, autos, chemicals, transport) most vulnerable to global slowdown. Multi-country refinancing walls (2026–27) now face repricing risk if growth expectations reset lower. Watch for CCC distress in capex-dependent sectors.

themeCards.title: CCC/distressed spread dislocation
themeCards.statusLine: CCC OAS spiked 18 bps to 1049 bps in a single day, signaling rapid repricing of tail risk. This occurred amid modest equity weakness (VIX +89 bps) and energy shock, suggesting liquidity or forced selling in structured credit.
themeCards.relevance: Distressed credit investors should hunt for dislocations in specific names (energy, retail, healthcare restructurings). CCC-to-B spread compression offers relative-value opportunities if volatility stabilizes. Monitor high-yield fallen angels in healthcare and specialty retail.

themeCards.title: Labor market inflection risk
themeCards.statusLine: August payrolls came in at -23K, a sharp miss from consensus +20K, marking first decline since early 2024. Unemployment held at 4.1%, but forward indicators (ISM employment, job openings) slowing sharply.
themeCards.relevance: If August was a trend reversal (not one-off), IG credit quality faces material deterioration in 2026–27. Leverage multiples expand; covenant cushions narrow. Watch September ADP (Sept 3) and October payrolls (Oct 3) for confirmation. Loan-loss provisions across finance, insurance, and mortgage servicers likely to rise.

ecb.delta: Hiked 25 bps in June 2026; base case no further hikes this year per market pricing.

chinaPMI.delta: August official NBS manufacturing PMI recovered 0.6 pts from July's 49.2, beating Reuters consensus of 49.6, but remains in contraction below 50.

ismServices.delta: July 2026 ISM Services PMI at 54.1 (slightly down from June's 54.0); August reading due Sept 5 will be key to assess service sector deceleration.

retailSales.delta: July 2026 retail sales ex-autos printed +5.75% YoY (prior +6.86%), showing continued but moderating growth. August detail unavailable.

existingHome.delta: July 2026 existing home sales slipped to 4.06M SAAR from 4.13M in June, marking second consecutive monthly decline but +0.7% YoY.

consensus.CPI: Expected ~3.2% YoY (Sept 2026 release, Aug data); recent inflation prints show cooling trend
consensus.Payrolls: Expected +120K–150K m/m for August (due Sept 4); prior miss of -23K signals caution
consensus.PCE: Expected ~3.1% headline YoY (Sept release, Aug data); core PCE likely ~2.5–2.6% YoY
consensus.PPI: Expected ~3.8–4.0% YoY (Sept release, Aug data); energy & commodity upside risks from Iran conflict
consensus.Retail Sales: Expected +0.3–0.5% m/m, ~3.5–4.0% YoY (Sept release, Aug data); sentiment weakness likely to weigh
consensus.ISM Mfg: Expected ~52–53 (Sept 1 release, Aug data); trend is toward softening; new orders critical
consensus.ISM Services: Expected ~52–54 (Sept 5 release, Aug data); services have held up better; June/July clues suggest slight softening
consensus.GDP: Q3 2026 GDPNow nowcast at 4.8%, but lagging Q2 actual 1.5%; consensus ~1.8–2.2% for Q3 GDP (delayed estimate)

regime.label: Late-cycle contraction risk
regime.detail: Inverted curve, sticky core inflation, faltering labor market, weakening global growth, and rising credit stress—classic pre-recession posture. Spreads compressing only modestly despite deterioration; defensive and distressed credit favored.
